slides.title: Purpose and use
bullets: For examining sputum in lower-respiratory-tract infection, Gram staining is recommended; the sputum or purulent sputum of a patient with an acute respiratory infection is examined in a Gram-stained smear.
The Ziehl–Neelsen method is given as the second way of staining sputum smears; the manual says any sputum may contain tubercle bacilli.
For staining the smear must be spread evenly and dried; for Gram it is fixed over a spirit-lamp flame.
This protocol contains only the steps given in the sources; the composition and preparation of the reagents are not given there — follow the laboratory’s approved instructions.

slides.title: Reagents and equipment
bullets: Gram method: gentian violet, Lugol’s solution, 90–95% alcohol, safranin; a spirit lamp for fixing.
Ziehl–Neelsen method: carbol-fuchsin (carbon-fuchsin) solution, acid alcohol, methylene blue; a cotton swab dipped in alcohol.
A staining rack (smears must not touch each other), a clock, water, immersion oil, a microscope.
Smears are tilted so that excess water runs off — leftover water interferes with the next dye.

slides.title: Gram staining
bullets: 1. Place the smear, fixed over the flame, on the staining rack and flood it with gentian violet — 1 minute.
2. Wash with water and shake off the excess.
3. Flood with Lugol’s solution (Aripova: 1 minute; Kurbonova: 30 seconds) and wash again.
4. Flood with 90–95% alcohol (Aripova: 30 seconds) and wash with water.
5. Flood with safranin (the Aripova text prints the time as “30–60 minutes”, which is clearly an error — take the time from the laboratory’s instructions) and wash with water.
6. Dry the smear at room temperature.

slides.title: Examining the Gram-stained smear
bullets: A few drops of oil are put on the smear and spread over its surface.
Aripova: first about 3 minutes are spent making sure the smear is even, then 10 minutes of careful examination; the type and number of all Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria are determined.
Gram-positive bacteria stain dark blue and Gram-negative ones red or pink; yeast-like cells stain dark blue and epithelial cells red or pink.
Normal: a few Gram-positive and Gram-negative cocci, diplococci, streptococci and rods — upper-respiratory-tract flora.

slides.title: Pathological findings (Gram smear)
rows: Gram-positive diplococci with an unstained capsule (clear halo)
Bronchopneumonia, acute lobar pneumonia, chronic bronchitis
Gram-negative diplococci inside and outside cells
Bronchopneumonia, for example in hospital after broad-spectrum antibiotics

slides.title: Ziehl–Neelsen staining
bullets: 1. Place several smears on the rack so that they do not touch; flood each with carbon-fuchsin solution.
2. Light a cotton swab dipped in alcohol and heat the slides evenly; as soon as steam appears set the clock for 5 minutes. Do not let the dye boil or overheat; if it begins to dry, add dye gently.
3. Pour off the dye and wash the smear gently with water until it is colourless; hold the slide tilted.
4. To decolourise, flood with acid alcohol for 3 minutes; wash gently with water.
5. Make sure the smear is completely decolourised; if traces of carbol-fuchsin remain, continue with acid alcohol.
6. Cover the smear with methylene blue for 30 seconds.

slides.title: Sources of error, reading and quality control
bullets: If the dye boils or overheats, or the slide is left dry, the staining is spoiled; leftover water interferes with the next dye.
If the smear is not fully decolourised, traces of carbol-fuchsin spoil the result.
How to read a Ziehl–Neelsen smear (colour, grading and counting) is not given in the source — use the laboratory’s approved instructions.
Internal quality control: keep a set of unstained smears made from positive sputum; check a new batch of dye or another reagent on a control smear stained together with every specimen.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Any sputum may contain tubercle bacilli: work in protective clothing.
Take care with open flame when lighting an alcohol-soaked swab; keep flammable liquids away from fire.
Wear gloves when handling dyes; used slides and solutions are disinfected.
